editor_spans.body: Read the four Ukraine statements in date order and the big thing they leave out is diesel. On 9 October the government responded to an 'agreement between US and Russia' without ever saying what was in it. Half of that response was about energy markets and the cost of living, not Ukraine.

Three days later the Prime Minister told the Commons why. The quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets is an energy ceasefire. He had pressed President Trump for one, and he welcomed it when it came. Britain's backing for the truce is about Kyiv's power grid, but it is also about fuel prices at home.

Two days after that, the leaders agreed that Russia had kept attacking civilians and energy infrastructure ever since Trump called for the truce. Britain's answer was more missiles, plus calls for others to 'ensure Russia heeds' the American call. That is a sign of how little say London has over a deal struck between Washington and Moscow.

The wording on Russian LNG is worth watching. The government says it is 'standing by plans to fully implement' the shipping and insurance ban, and is urging partners to do the same. You don't need to say you are standing by a plan unless people are asking whether you will drop it. When energy prices are the worry, a ban that squeezes gas supply is the first thing under pressure. The question that matters is whether it holds through the winter, not how firmly ministers talk about it now.

Look at the timing of the Great British Railways headquarters. Building starts in early 2027 and finishes in spring 2029, close to when the next general election is due. The 'hundreds of jobs' are really up to 450 staff moving into one office. So the HQ will be a ribbon-cutting just before voters decide, not an early result of public ownership.

The workforce problem is bigger than the announcement makes it sound. Under 7% of rail workers are under 25. Up to 600 apprentices over four years is about 150 a year, spread across a national industry. That is a gesture, not a fix. The best things in this package for Derby are the Alstom train orders and the city's existing role as a rail hub. The headquarters mainly adds a symbol to them.

Burnham is offering Scotland the idea that made him: power pushed down to regions and cities, run through his own No10 North operation. He presents it as cooperation, but the case for it is an attack on Holyrood. It says the Scottish Government is one of Europe's most centralised devolved administrations, and that power 'was never supposed to stop' at its doors. In practice, Westminster would be building direct links with Scottish regions that go around Edinburgh.

His Scottish Secretary names London and Edinburgh side by side as places ministers decide things they shouldn't. That puts Westminster and Holyrood on the same footing. A First Minister will find that hard to accept. The 'offer' looks designed as much to set up an argument as to be taken up.
